facts.label: My role
facts.value: Requirements, edge cases and approvals; AI tools did the implementation

banner.title: Messy records in. Traceable data out.
banner.alt: Before and after. Before: rows from the fictional sample input, where one has a blank ID, one has the date 2024-02-30, one says N/A for quantity, one has the category “Pressure Unit” and one repeats another row’s ID. After: clean records with standard categories, and an exceptions file holding rows for a person with their reasons.
banner.caption: Real rows from this project’s fictional sample data.

situation: Before inventory moves into a new system, someone has to decide what every messy record means. Guess wrong and a pump gets quoted as a sensor, or a quantity nobody entered quietly becomes zero.
This project rebuilds that problem with 60 fictional equipment records and one rule: when the data can’t decide, a person does.

decisions.title: Flag, don’t fix.
decisions.body: A category like “pressure unit” could mean a pump or a sensor. Instead of picking one, the row goes to a person with the reason attached. It’s slower, but an ambiguous category is never resolved silently.
decisions.term: Exact alias matching; no fuzzy matching.

visual.alt: Illustration: the label “pressure unit” could point to a pump or a sensor, so the row is sent to human review.

decisions.title: Accept one date format.
decisions.body: 03/04/2024 is March 4 to one reader and April 3 to another, and an impossible date like February 30th looks normal at a glance. Only real calendar dates written as YYYY-MM-DD get through.
decisions.term: Strict `YYYY-MM-DD` with ASCII digits; impossible dates rejected.

visual.alt: Illustration: 03/04/2024 reads as March 4 in the US and April 3 in the UK, so the date is rejected rather than guessed.

decisions.title: Reject every copy of a duplicated ID.
decisions.body: When two rows claim the same ID, nothing in the data says which one is real, so neither is kept. Rejecting only the second copy would quietly trust whichever happened to come first.

text: All 60 rows are accounted for: 37 clean records and 23 held for review, each with its reason. Run it twice and you get the same files.

next: A simple review screen: each held row with its reason and the closest likely match shown, with the final call left to the reviewer.

notes: Input and mapping files are checked for structural problems before anything is written; a malformed file stops the run with exit code 2, while bad rows become reviewable exceptions.
Every input row gets exactly one outcome, and `summary.json` reconciles input = accepted + rejected.
A blank quantity is missing, while an explicit `0` is a valid count; neither is defaulted.
Exceptions keep the source row number, the raw values and every error code, so a reviewer sees exactly what arrived.
Outputs carry no timestamps, so a rerun is byte-for-byte identical.
Standard-library Python at runtime; 21 pytest tests, including a small fixture whose expected output was worked out by hand.

story.headline: When shipping everything isn’t worth it
story.lede: A small optimization model that weighs the cost of a shortage against the cost of opening another container, and checks every plan it produces.

facts.label: My role
facts.value: Requirements, edge cases and approvals; AI tools did the implementation

facts.label: Built with
facts.value: Python, PuLP with the CBC solver, pytest

banner.title: Only the normal scenario ships every requested unit
banner.alt: Stacked bars of units shipped and short out of 309 requested: normal 309 shipped; high shortage penalty 130 shipped and 179 short; tight capacity 112 shipped and 197 short; low shortage penalty and no inventory 0 shipped and 309 short.
banner.caption: Results from the five fictional scenarios in the repo. Costs are in made-up units, not real freight rates.

situation: Opening a shipping container has a fixed cost. Sometimes leaving a few units behind is cheaper than paying for another container, and sometimes it isn’t, so the right answer depends on the numbers.
This project models that trade-off with four fictional products and two containers, and tests it under five scenarios, from normal capacity to no stock at all.

decisions.title: Use a proven method, not a rule of thumb.
decisions.body: Which containers to open, and what to put in them, is a known kind of problem: a fixed-charge allocation. Writing it as an integer program states the trade-off exactly and lets an established solver find the answer, instead of a hand-tuned rule.
decisions.term: Integer program; PuLP with the CBC solver; yes-or-no container decisions.

visual.alt: Illustration: “Which containers should we open?” is recognized as a known fixed-charge allocation problem, so a proven method is used.

decisions.title: Say what the model leaves out.
decisions.body: The model checks weight and volume, not how boxes actually stack. A container can be 100% full by volume on paper and still not pack, so every output states that it is not a loading plan.
decisions.term: Mass and volume limits only; no 3D packing, stacking or load restraint.

visual.alt: Illustration: a container 100% full by volume and 82% by weight may still not pack in 3D; the model keeps weight and volume and states that limit in every output.

decisions.title: Check the solver’s answer.
decisions.body: A solver can stop early or return values with tiny numerical errors. Separate code re-checks every plan against stock, demand, weight and volume and recomputes its cost. A plan is reported as OPTIMAL only when the solver reports an optimum and that check passes.
decisions.term: Independent `check_plan`; `FEASIBLE` when there is no optimality proof.

text: Across the five scenarios the model behaves as the trade-off predicts. With normal containers every unit ships; with small containers some demand goes unmet, and raising the shortage penalty ships more of it; with tiny penalties, shipping nothing is cheapest. Reruns in the same environment produce byte-identical output.

next: Add a simple packing check for the containers the model chooses, which would mean adding the item dimensions the model doesn’t have yet.

notes: For every product, shipped units plus shortage equal demand, and shipments never exceed stock.
The objective is shortage penalties plus fixed container charges, all in fictional `toy_cost_units`.
A hand-checkable example in the README (five units, one container) has a unique optimum of 42, and the tests confirm it.
A solver stop that returns a valid but unproven plan is labelled `FEASIBLE`, not `OPTIMAL`; unit tests cover this status mapping, and an independent review checked real CBC time-limit stops.
130 pytest tests; reruns in the same environment write byte-identical JSON (tested) and text output.
PuLP is pinned to 3.3.2 because PuLP 4.2.0 failed in the tested environment.

story.headline: Usage metrics that mean one thing
story.lede: A small dashboard that validates raw event logs first, then turns them into daily activity, module usage and an ordered funnel, each with its definition written down.

facts.label: My role
facts.value: Requirements, edge cases and approvals; AI tools did the implementation

banner.title: Raw clicks in. Clear answers out.
banner.alt: Before and after. Before: rows from the fictional event log, with time, user, module and action, fading into “5,766 rows like these”. After: a dashboard showing 175 users in scope, 1,520 sessions and 619 full-funnel sessions, with a September daily active users chart where weekends are shaded.
banner.caption: Redrawn from this project’s fictional event data; the rows and numbers are real, the layout is simplified.

situation: “How many people use the product?” sounds like one question. Daily users, total events and funnel progress give three different answers, and a duplicated or malformed event can quietly change all of them.
This project explores that problem with 28 days of fictional events from an invented B2B web app.

decisions.title: Validate the whole file before any filter.
decisions.body: Exact duplicate events collapse to one, conflicting copies are quarantined and rows with missing or invalid fields are rejected, all before any date or module filter is applied. Changing the view never changes what counts as valid data.
decisions.term: File-wide validation; every raw row gets exactly one outcome.

visual.alt: Illustration: all modules for September 1–28 show 5,735 events and catalog for one week shows 480, but the 31 rows not counted stay the same under any filter, because validation runs on the whole file first.

decisions.title: Write down every denominator.
decisions.body: Daily active users are distinct people per day, not the sum of each module’s users, and module share is a share of events, not of people. Each chart states what it counts, and a rate shows N/A instead of a misleading zero when there is nothing to divide by.
decisions.term: Distinct users, events and sessions kept separate; N/A for empty denominators.

decisions.title: Count a funnel step only if it happens later.
decisions.body: A session reaches the next step only when that action happens strictly after the previous one. Repeated clicks don’t count twice, and two actions in the same second don’t prove an order.
decisions.term: Session = a (user, session) pair; strictly increasing timestamps.

text: Of 5,766 raw rows, 5,735 are valid and every other row is accounted for: 10 duplicate copies collapsed, 8 quarantined and 13 rejected. In September, 1,357 sessions opened a page, 844 then searched and 619 then viewed a detail: 46% of the sessions that opened a page.

next: Let users choose the funnel steps and add sessions based on inactivity, so the same definitions can answer more questions.

notes: Every raw row has exactly one outcome: 5,766 raw = 5,735 valid + 10 collapsed + 8 quarantined + 13 rejected.
Timestamps must be `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` in UTC with ASCII digits; other offsets are rejected, not converted.
Date filters include the start date from midnight UTC and stop at midnight after the end date.
The metric code has no Streamlit dependency, so another interface could reuse the same definitions.
A seeded generator produces byte-identical data on every run; 44 pytest tests, including headless dashboard runs.

story.headline: Counting demand once
story.lede: A hypothetical systems design for a small distributor that keeps quotes, orders, reservations and shipments as separate facts, each with one owner.

facts.label: My role
facts.value: Requirements, edge cases and approvals; AI tools produced the documents and checks

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: A proposed design, not a built system

banner.title: Same order, three numbers. One meaning each.
banner.alt: Before and after. Before: three sticky notes read quote 4 units, order 2 units and shipped 1 unit, and a report adds them into “4 + 2 + 1 = 7 units” of demand, crossed out. After: the same order as countable squares, 4 quoted, 2 ordered and 1 shipped, giving demand 2, shipped 1 and owed 1.
banner.caption: Illustration: the “4 + 2 + 1” total is the kind of double counting this design is meant to rule out. The order itself comes from the case study’s fictional scenario.

situation: One customer request can show up three times: as a quote for 4 units, an order for 2 and a shipment of 1. Add them up and a report shows far more demand than anyone committed to.
This case study designs, on paper, how a small fictional distributor could keep those facts apart, and checks its own numbers with small scripts.

decisions.title: Give every fact one owner.
decisions.body: Quotes belong to Quotation, orders and their status to Orders, and stock and shipments to Inventory and Fulfillment. Other modules can read a fact but not edit it, so an order can’t be “closed” in one place and “partly shipped” in another.
decisions.term: Modular monolith; Reporting reads everything and owns no source facts.

visual.alt: Illustration: a quote for 4 units, an order for 2 and a shipment of 1 are different facts; adding 4 + 2 gives a wrong 6 units of demand, and committed demand is 2.

decisions.title: Count demand from accepted orders only.
decisions.body: Committed demand is the 2 units on the accepted order. The 4 quoted units are reported separately as a signal, and shipping changes what’s still owed, not demand. Each record keeps the ID of the one it came from, so demand and conversion numbers can be traced back to the records they came from.
decisions.term: Identifier lineage: order line → quote line → opportunity.

decisions.title: Reserve stock at the order, not the quote.
decisions.body: Many quotes never convert, so a quote doesn’t hold stock; only an accepted order can reserve it. The cost is written down too: a customer told “in stock” when quoting may find that only part of the order can ship right away.
decisions.term: Architecture decision record ADR-001; worth revisiting for scarce or made-to-order items.

text: The scenario’s numbers reconcile: 4 quoted, 2 ordered, 1 shipped and 1 still owed, and committed demand stays at 2 even after the second unit ships in the walkthrough. A small calculator and a document checker confirm the arithmetic and that every identifier in the documents exists in the data.

next: Build a small prototype of the Orders and Inventory modules to test what the design leaves open, such as keeping reservations consistent when two orders arrive at once.

notes: Remaining quantity is derived (ordered − shipped) and never edited by hand; cancellations and returns are out of scope.
Estimates, observed facts and missing values are tagged separately, and a missing arrival date is never treated as zero days.
Five metric definitions each state their unit, population and denominator; win rate counts opportunities, while conversion counts units.
Three short architecture decision records give the context, decision and consequences of each choice.
Standard-library Python only: a scenario calculator, a document checker and 30 unit tests.
One SKU, one warehouse and five invented cohort rows; the numbers illustrate arithmetic, not business performance.

homePreview.eyebrow: Academic foundations · Applied mathematics and philosophy
homePreview.title: Applied Thinking: The reasoning behind the work
homePreview.description: My background in applied mathematics and philosophy informs how I approach unfamiliar problems: recognizing useful structures, separating what can be established from what remains uncertain, tracing dependencies, and testing assumptions before trusting conclusions.
homePreview.supportingText: Mathematics offers methods for representing and analyzing a problem; philosophy offers complementary ways to examine the assumptions, evidence and interpretations behind those methods. The value is in combining both with domain knowledge and practical validation.

hero.title: Applied Thinking: Mathematics, Philosophy & Practical Problem-Solving
hero.tagline: Understanding what can be modeled, what can be inferred, and what remains uncertain.
paragraphs: A mathematical method can be correct for the problem it was given while the problem itself is poorly specified. A plausible explanation can fit the observed evidence without being established fact. And a simplified model can be useful while still concealing an important dependency.

My academic background gives me complementary tools for these situations: applied mathematics for identifying structure and constructing models, and philosophy for examining assumptions, justification, uncertainty and the limits of those models.

foundations.title: Structural reasoning
foundations.body: Applied mathematics trains the habit of representing a problem through variables, relationships, constraints and conditions. A useful framework often begins with the recognition that a type of problem has already been studied—even when the specific theorem or method must be researched again. This invites the questions: What structure is present? What conditions must hold? What can be solved or bounded?

foundations.title: Epistemic reasoning
foundations.body: Philosophy examines how concepts are defined, what counts as evidence, how inferences are justified, and what remains unclear. It asks whether an apparent solution actually answers the intended question and whether the assumptions behind the model are warranted. It also helps distinguish not knowing a system’s internals from having no evidence about its behavior.

appliedThinking.sharedConcern: Neither discipline eliminates the need for domain expertise. Together they support clearer problem formulation and more careful evaluation of what a model or explanation can actually establish.

principles.title: Recognizing Applicable Frameworks
principles.question: Does this unfamiliar problem belong to a class that already has useful methods?
principles.explanation: The starting point is not always remembering a formula. It may be recognizing that an assignment task resembles matching, that a shipping problem has an optimization structure, or that a workflow is a network of dependencies. That recognition makes it possible to research the appropriate tool instead of starting from nothing.
principles.method: Define the variables and objective, identify candidate methods, then verify their assumptions and limitations before using them.
principles.academicConnections: Operations Research, mathematical modeling, Real Analysis; theorems and their hypotheses.
principles.limitation: Recognizing a possible framework is not proof that the framework is applicable or that domain expertise can be skipped.

visual.alt: Recognizing frameworks: “Which containers should we open?” is a known fixed-charge allocation problem, so a proven method (PuLP with the CBC solver) is used instead of a new rule of thumb.

principles.title: Narrowing Ambiguity
principles.question: What can be established now, and what needs additional evidence or human judgment?
principles.explanation: Complex projects contain both well-specified cases and ambiguous exceptions. I favor establishing boundaries and handling cases whose rules can be validated before spending effort on unresolved ones. The remainder becomes a focused list of questions rather than a mixture of guesses and apparently finished work.
principles.method: State assumptions, separate deterministic transformations from conditional inferences, preserve exceptions, and revise the boundary as new information arrives.
principles.academicConnections: Constraint reasoning, iterative numerical methods, optimization, logical distinctions.
principles.limitation: The process does not promise mathematical convergence or that every ambiguity can be removed.

visual.alt: Narrowing ambiguity: is a “pressure unit” a pump or a sensor? The data can’t decide, so the row is sent to human review instead of guessed.

principles.title: Decomposing and Reconnecting Systems
principles.question: Which subproblems can be handled separately, and which dependencies must remain visible?
principles.explanation: A complicated problem is often easier to work with as a set of smaller problems. But solving the parts independently can fail if the relationships between them are lost. A graph-like view helps track shared dependencies, interfaces, exceptions and how local decisions affect the system as a whole.
principles.method: Identify nodes and relationships, examine ownership and handoffs, solve tractable subproblems, then reconnect the results and check consistency.
principles.academicConnections: Network Models, graph theory, systems modeling, recursive decomposition.
principles.limitation: A hierarchy is not always a tree; real workflows may contain shared dependencies, feedback and cycles.

visual.alt: Decomposing systems: a quote for 4 units, an order for 2 and a shipment of 1 are different facts. Adding 4 + 2 gives a wrong 6 units of demand; committed demand is 2.

principles.title: Testing What Remains True
principles.question: Which features of a conclusion survive when the problem changes?
principles.explanation: Changing a constraint, representation or input can reveal whether a conclusion depends on essential structure or an accidental choice. Some mathematical properties are invariant under defined transformations; in applied work, sensitivity and robustness tests serve a related—but not identical—purpose.
principles.method: Vary one assumption at a time, look for thresholds and failure cases, and record when the original reasoning stops applying.
principles.academicConnections: Linear Algebra, Real Analysis, sensitivity analysis, topology as a conceptual connection.
principles.limitation: Passing a few scenarios is not a proof of invariance or universal robustness.

visual.alt: Testing what remains true: changing one input at a time. Normal: both containers open, 309 units ship. Smaller containers: only the large one opens, 112 ship. Smaller containers with penalties times 4: both open, 130 ship. Tiny penalties: none open, 0 ship, because all shortages together cost 288.5, less than the cheapest opening charge (400).

principles.title: Examining the Reasoning Behind Evidence
principles.question: Could a reasoning error affect not only a conclusion but also the way evidence is collected or interpreted?
principles.explanation: A logical mistake can occur before any calculation begins. If evidence is selected using an unjustified assumption, a sophisticated method may produce internally consistent results from a distorted picture of the world. The genetic fallacy illustrates the danger of treating the origin of a claim as decisive proof of its truth or falsity.
principles.method: Separate provenance from claim validity, inspect operational definitions, examine how data were selected, and distinguish observations from inferences.
principles.academicConnections: Symbolic Logic, Philosophy of Science, epistemology and philosophy of scientific method.
principles.limitation: Source reliability often matters; using provenance as evidence about reliability is not itself a fallacy.

visual.alt: Examining evidence: all modules for September 1–28 show 5,735 events and catalog for one week shows 480, but the 31 rows not counted stay the same under any filter, because validation runs on the whole file first.

principles.title: Simplifying Without Losing What Matters
principles.question: How much complexity can be removed before a representation becomes misleading?
principles.explanation: Reduction is unavoidable in practical modeling. A simplified inventory model may be enough to compare resource allocations while being insufficient to certify real packing or operational feasibility. A good abstraction is evaluated against the question it must answer, not by how little detail it contains.
principles.method: State the decision the model supports, identify omitted behavior, test whether key relationships survive, and make limitations visible.
principles.academicConnections: Philosophical reductionism, mathematical abstraction, dimensionality reduction, numerical linear algebra.
principles.limitation: Preserving one decision-relevant property does not mean all properties were preserved.

visual.alt: Simplifying responsibly: a container can be 100% full by volume and 82% by weight on paper and still not pack in 3D. The model keeps weight and volume, leaves out 3D packing and says so in every output.

principles.title: Choosing Under Uncertainty
principles.question: Which explanation should guide action when the available evidence is incomplete?
principles.explanation: Abductive reasoning compares competing explanations and asks which best accounts for what is known. It is useful in troubleshooting and exploratory research, where a single observation may be consistent with several causes. A provisional explanation can guide the next test without becoming an established fact.
principles.method: Generate alternatives, ask what evidence would distinguish them, examine the costs of further investigation, and choose actions while communicating uncertainty.
principles.academicConnections: Abductive reasoning, Probability, Bayesian updating as a possible formal tool, decision theory.
principles.limitation: The most plausible explanation is not necessarily true; the best-supported explanation and the best action may differ.

visual.alt: Choosing under uncertainty, a conceptual illustration: a shipment is late, and three causes fit. Supplier shipped late, decided by the ship date; carrier was slow, decided by the transit time; wrong date on file, decided by the order history. The likeliest cause guides the next check but stays a hypothesis.

principles.title: Managing What Cannot Be Fully Understood
principles.question: How can a complex system be evaluated when some internal details remain inaccessible or hard to interpret?
principles.explanation: Opacity has different causes: hidden information, complicated dependencies, computational limits, poorly documented interfaces, or difficult-to-interpret model internals. Those problems require different responses. Sometimes the appropriate goal is deeper explanation; sometimes it is bounded behavioral testing, observable interfaces, independent checks or explicit human review.
principles.method: Identify the type of opacity, clarify the required assurance, introduce tests and documentation, and avoid claiming understanding beyond the available evidence.
principles.academicConnections: Epistemology, philosophy of science, systems modeling, numerical verification.
principles.limitation: Validated behavior is not the same as mechanistic interpretability, and no limited test suite proves universal correctness.

visual.alt: Managing opaque systems: headless tests give the dashboard a test file with known answers and check the numbers shown in the app: 17 valid events, 6 rejected and 2 quarantined rows.

connections.title: Frameworks and justification
connections.body: The existence of an established method answers how one might solve the problem. It does not answer whether this problem satisfies the method’s conditions.

connections.title: Decomposition and reductionism
connections.body: Breaking a system into parts helps make it tractable. Evaluating what the split excludes protects against a locally correct but globally misleading solution.

connections.title: Boundaries and uncertain inference
connections.body: Deterministic checks can narrow the unresolved space; abduction helps evaluate the explanations that remain when the evidence does not uniquely settle them.

connections.title: Perturbation and opacity
connections.body: Changing inputs or assumptions can test observable behavior without requiring full access to the internal mechanism. It does not eliminate all hidden failure modes.

connections.title: Models and decisions
connections.body: A mathematical model can rank feasible choices against its stated objective; philosophy and domain judgment are needed to examine whether the objective is appropriate in the first place.

workflow.title: Approaching an unfamiliar domain
workflow.intro: There is no guaranteed sequence that solves every unfamiliar problem. The following operations are reusable and often iterative:

steps.title: Clarify the decision
steps.body: Identify the stakeholder’s question, not just the available data or requested calculation.

steps.title: Locate the structure
steps.body: Look for recognizable problem classes, variables, dependencies and constraints.

steps.title: Separate the known from the unresolved
steps.body: Handle verifiable rules and isolate ambiguous cases without guessing.

steps.title: Model and investigate
steps.body: Select a method whose assumptions fit; seek domain expertise when needed.

steps.title: Perturb and validate
steps.body: Change assumptions, compare alternatives, test edge cases and review omitted information.

steps.title: Explain what follows
steps.body: Communicate the conclusion, evidence, uncertainty and next decision.

workflow.closing: A later discovery may send the process back to an earlier step. Adaptability is not the absence of learning curves; it is having a structured way to find and navigate them.

caseStudyBridges.label: Data quality — Deciding what not to automate
caseStudyBridges.body: The Synthetic Data Quality Pipeline distinguishes valid zero values from missing data and routes ambiguous category mappings to exceptions. It illustrates how the boundary between deterministic transformation and unsupported inference can be made explicit. This synthetic Python project is separate from professional inventory migration work.

caseStudyBridges.label: Shipping optimization — Explicit trade-offs and fragile assumptions
caseStudyBridges.body: The Inventory and Shipping Optimization Lab represents a narrow fictional allocation problem through constraints and an objective, then tests multiple scenarios and checks solver output independently. The model deliberately does not claim full container packing or production freight optimization.

caseStudyBridges.label: Product analytics — Definitions before dashboards
caseStudyBridges.body: The Product Usage Analytics Demo distinguishes event counts, distinct users and funnel progression while documenting filters, denominators and invalid records. It illustrates that measured quantities must be defined relative to the business question before a chart can be trusted.

caseStudyBridges.label: B2B systems — Preserving business distinctions
caseStudyBridges.body: The B2B Sales Systems Case Study separates quotations, commitments, reservations and shipments in a hypothetical architecture. This makes responsibility and system boundaries clearer; it is a hypothetical design, not a deployed system.

rows.title: Operations Research
rows.translation: Like packing a moving truck on a budget: finding the best plan among the ones that actually fit. The shipping optimization project uses one of its standard tools, integer programming, to weigh the cost of unshipped units against the cost of opening another container.

rows.title: Mathematical Modeling
rows.translation: Like drawing a map before a trip: decide what goes on it, what to leave off, then check the map against the road. Every project here starts by writing down what its model assumes.

rows.title: Network Models
rows.translation: Like a subway map: it shows what connects to what, so you can see where a delay spreads. The B2B case study uses this to trace how a quote, an order and a shipment depend on each other.

rows.title: Probability
rows.translation: Like a weather forecast: a calibrated guess you update as conditions change. It’s also how AI models work: they generate a probable answer, not a guaranteed one. In practice, it means keeping estimates labelled as estimates, revising them when facts arrive, and checking AI output rather than taking it as fact.

rows.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
rows.translation: Like a bathtub filling and draining at the same time: the level depends on both rates over time, not just where it started. Useful for anything that accumulates, like stock, users or backlogs.

rows.title: Real Analysis
rows.translation: If calculus is learning to drive, real analysis is learning how the engine works, and when it won’t start. In practice, it means checking a method’s conditions before trusting its answer.

rows.title: Multivariable Analysis (Spivak, Calculus on Manifolds)
rows.translation: Real analysis explains the engine; this explains how the whole vehicle handles when steering, throttle and brakes change at once, and proves when a small adjustment has a predictable effect. In practice: judging when a simple estimate of how a result responds to many inputs can be trusted, and which conclusions don’t depend on how the problem is set up (see {principle}).

rows.title: Topology
rows.translation: Why a coffee mug and a donut count as the same shape: it studies what stays true when you bend and stretch something without tearing it. Behind it is a habit of asking which conclusions survive when the inputs change (see {principle}).

rows.title: Numerical Linear Algebra
rows.translation: The engine room of spreadsheets, search and machine learning: how computers work with huge tables of numbers fast, without rounding errors piling up. It explains why two correct-looking calculations can disagree.

rows.title: Symbolic Logic
rows.translation: Grammar for arguments: it checks whether a conclusion really follows, however convincing it sounds. It helps spot a requirement or claim that doesn’t follow from its evidence.

rows.title: Philosophy of Science
rows.translation: How to tell a good test from a lucky one: what counts as evidence, and how a method can fool you. It’s why every result on this site says how it was checked.

rows.title: High Performance Computing
rows.translation: How to make computers solve large problems faster by splitting the work across many processors at once. Much of the difficulty isn’t the arithmetic but moving data: keeping it close to the processor that needs it and limiting how often processors wait on each other. It’s about knowing when a correct method will be too slow or costly at scale.

appliedThinking.disclosure: The professional responsibilities described elsewhere on this site concern real work. The linked demonstrations are separate public artifacts using fictional data and reduced scope. Their outputs and test results do not measure employer systems or business outcomes.
appliedThinking.closing: This page describes transferable reasoning foundations, not a guarantee that a particular method works in every domain. Professional decisions still depend on appropriate evidence, stakeholder priorities, technical implementation and domain knowledge. The case studies show selected applications or analogues with their assumptions and limitations made explicit.
